newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Amnesty wants arms flow to Zaire conflict stopped.
newsitem.headline: Amnesty wants arms flow to Zaire conflict stopped.

text.p: Human rights group Amnesty International called on Monday for the international community to stop the flow of arms to Central Africa, where they are being used in atrocities by all sides in the Zaire conflict.

Amnesty Secretary-General Pierre Sane, on a visit to South Africa, said foreign weapons were being used in abuses carried out by all parties to the fighting along Zaire's eastern border with Rwanda and Burundi.
Weapons and ammunition should be prevented from reaching the armed forces, militias and other armed groups in Zaire, Burundi and Rwanda, he said in a statement.
"The situation is an explosive and catastrophic one affecting countless refugess and civilians in these countries.
"It has been widely acknowledged that the area is awash with small arms despite previous commitments by the international community to restrict them," the statement said.

"Recent reports of deliberate and arbitrary killings and other grave abuses committed by Zairean soldiers and the Banyamulenge (Tutsi) armed opposition in eastern Zaire are part of a much broader pattern of atrocities carried out to a greater or lesser extent by all sides in the conflict along the Zairean border with Rwanda and Burundi," Sane said.

South Africa has come in for criticism for agreeing to arms sales worth an estimated 86.8 million rand ($18.5 million) to Rwanda's military government, and Pretoria has announced a review of its September decision to lift an arms ban on the Central African country.

Sane said the Great Lakes region was awash with weapons from various countries including Belgium, China, Chile, Egypt, France, Germany, Israel, Romania, Russia, South Africa, the United States and Yugoslavia.
"There have been arms deliveries to Zaire, Burundi and Rwanda despite serious human rights abuses by the armed forces and associated militia, especially in the border areas," the statement said.
Rivalry between majority Hutus and minority ethnic Tutsis has troubled Rwanda and Burundi for generations and has now spilled on to the territory of mineral-rich Zaire.
Foreign armies have denied fighting alongside Tutsi rebels in Zaire but Rwanda has said it sent troops on an incursion this week after artillery and machinegun exchanges across its border.
Around one million ethnic Hutu refugees in war-torn eastern Zaire have been on the move as fighting between Tutsi rebels and Zairean troops raged.
Aid workers said the displaced people had begun to move west from the world's largest refugee camp at Mugunga deeper into Zaire.
Zaire accuses Tutsi-led Rwanda, which has long complained of cross-border raids by Hutu hardliners living among the refugees, of sending troops to fight alongside the rebels.
